newsitem.title: GERMANY: FEATURE - German unemployment hits prisons too.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - German unemployment hits prisons too.

text.p: Germany is suffering its worst employment crisis since the 1930s and it is not just long-pampered workers who have priced themselves out of a job.
Prison labourers are finding their jobs being taken by cheaper competition abroad.

In the last few months between 50 and 60 prisoners have lost their jobs at Diez prison near Limburg, as several firms, including a large German car company, pulled out and moved operations to Poland and the Czech Republic.
"In the late 1980s we used to have almost full employment here. But now only about half of the prisoners have work," said prison work director Michael Haberstock.
"It is just the same behind the prison walls as it is outside," added prison director Dieter Bandell. "We are losing jobs to cheaper labour in eastern Europe."
Prison labour is admittedly subject to a few restrictive practices -- security dictates that firms must bring their machinery behind the jail walls and prisoners cannot work night shifts.
But they still offer a deal most employers would die for.

Companies do not have to pay their prison workers the array of welfare contributions which are blamed for much of Germany's lack of competitiveness, and they can choose each day how many staff they need, without having to compensate anyone.
Wages are just 100 marks ($61) a day, the minimum wage for manual work but in reality well below the going rate "outside". The prisoners get to keep one tenth.
"I find it unbelievable that it can be cheaper for a firm to move to eastern Europe, build a new plant and then transport its goods back to Germany," said Haberstock.
JAIL "UNEMPLOYMENT" 50 PERCENT IN SOME CASES

While German unemployment outside has reached a record 4.16 million, or 10.8 percent, and is still rising, jail "unemployment" has hit 50 percent in some prisons, leaving many inmates shut in their cells for up to 23 hours a day.

German law states that life in prison should be as similar as possible to life outside and work has long been considered an essential part of the rehabilitation of criminals. It is also a valuable source of income for the state.
"It gets the men used to working, gives them something to be proud of and means they have a better relationship with the guards," said Bandell.

"Unemployment outside has a double effect for us. Firstly unemployment brings social problems and more crime and so more prisoners, and secondly it means that it is more difficult to find them work when they are here," said Haberstock.
In the last few years Diez has been forced to take in 60 to 70 more prisoners than its capacity of 480, forcing many prisoners to share the tiny cells.
Although the Federal Justice Ministry in Bonn could give no figure of the national extent of joblessness in German prisons, states across Germany are reporting the problem.
The justice ministry of Saxony said that at Bautzen, one of the largest prisons in eastern Germany, 45 percent of prisoners had no work.
"We are certainly noticing that fewer businesses want to come into prisons," said spokesman Friedrich Stolberg.
Just like people on the outside, prisoners are keen to hang on to their jobs.

Although income from work amounts to only 200 to 300 marks a month, prisoners can decide to spend that money how they choose, sending it to their family, saving to buy a television, or paying off old debts.
Unemployed prisoners, who receive only 50 marks pocket money each month, must spend it all in the prison shop and may not save for when they are released.
"Of course there is envy between prisoners who have money and those that don't, just like outside," said Peter K., a 33-year-old prisoner, who lost his job last month.
"I have heart problems and the doctor said it isn't good for me to be sitting in my cell all day," he said.
DIFFICULT TO COMPETE WITH CHEAP LABOUR ABOAD
Bandell said that, because prisons were not allowed to cut pay below the minimum wage, there was little they could do to compete with cheaper labour abroad.

"We try to offer those without work sport, discussion groups, or classes, but for that we need more staff. Also if unemployed prisoners are having a good time then those with jobs will think 'Why should I be so stupid and work all day?'"
Haberstock said that even when the German economy picked up it would be difficult to find firms who wanted to come back behind the barbed wire.
"Many manual jobs have been automated and many prisoners are not qualified to do more high technology jobs," he said.
Just as a shorter working week and less overtime are being touted as solutions to the national problem, Bandell suggested that prisoners may have to go in for "job-sharing" in future.

He left no doubt that the frustrations of unemployment were little different inside jail and outside, and said the rehabilitation of thousands of criminals would be hampered and jails could become more violent if more work was not found.
"Prisoners without work are like tigers in a cage," he said. ($1=1.6383 Mark)
